name: responsive-design
context: One product must be served to phones, tablets, laptops, televisions and embedded screens that differ in viewport width, pixel density, input modality, network class and CPU budget — and the decision is not whether to adapt, it is *where in the delivery path* adaptation happens. That placement is an architecture decision with hard, non-obvious consequences, because each option moves cost and risk to a different component. Adapting entirely in the client with CSS media queries keeps one cacheable document and one backend, but ships layout work and often an oversized hero image to a device that cannot use it. Adapting at the server (branching the render, or serving a separate m.example.com) lets you send only what the device class needs, but it multiplies rendered variants, multiplies the cache key, and makes the origin — not the CDN — pay for every request. Negotiating at the edge with HTTP Client Hints keeps the origin device-agnostic and pushes media transformation to a CDN tier, but only pays off if the cache is configured for it: a response that varies on Sec-CH-DPR without the URL carrying a file extension, or without Vary set correctly, will be served BYPASS or cached wrongly. The historical failure mode was User-Agent sniffing, which requires an ever-growing device database, misfires on every new browser, and is trivially spoofable — the platform answer (Client Hints) only partly fixes it, because MDN's own guidance is that changing site *functionality* on client hints is still a bad idea and capability detection should be preferred.
benefits: One URL space and one codebase for every device class, so there is no m.example.com to keep in sync and no second front-end codebase to staff
Adaptation is placed deliberately — in the client, the origin, or the edge — instead of accumulating as ad-hoc UA checks scattered through rendering code
Client-hint negotiation moves per-variant media work (resize, format, DPR) to a CDN tier where it is cheap and cacheable, instead of to the origin on every request
A `Vary` on the negotiated hints multiplies the cache key deliberately rather than accidentally, so a cache hit rate can be measured and tuned instead of collapsing to a single shared entry

Container queries let a component adapt to the width of the slot it is placed in rather than to the viewport, which is what makes a shared design system reusable in a three-column desktop layout and a one-column phone layout
The same structure degrades: a viewport-width layout with breakpoints is a strict superset of the one-column mobile case, so a failed upgrade costs readability, not function
tradeoffs: Every dimension negotiated on the server adds a header, a cache variant and an origin render path — MDN notes server-driven negotiation 'doesn't scale well' because one header per feature is needed and each is sent on every request
Shared caches get less effective as representations multiply: MDN lists reduced shared-cache efficiency and more complex server implementations as the standing costs of content negotiation

Client-hint negotiation is opt-in and asymmetric: the server must send `Accept-CH` before the client will send hints, hints are available only on secure origins, and `DPR`/`Width`/`Viewport-Width` still do not cover every capability a decision might want

Adapting by rendering variant at the origin moves device-class branching into the render path, which reintroduces exactly the cache-miss and layout-duplication problem the single-document approach avoids
Container queries are broadly available but are a different mental model from media queries; a codebase half-migrated has two breakpoints systems that interact unpredictably

Responsive layouts multiply the states a design must be checked in — every breakpoint crossed with every orientation crossed with every input modality, which is a test-matrix cost, not just a design cost
Negotiated formats and DPR variants multiply stored objects and invalidate them on every source change, so a media pipeline becomes an operational concern with cache-busting rules
use_cases: A single e-commerce or content site serving phones, tablets and desktops from one URL space with one render path
Media-heavy pages where hero and thumbnail images dominate transfer and belong to an edge transformation pipeline keyed on Sec-CH-DPR and Sec-CH-Width
Static or SSR sites that need an art-directed crop at a breakpoint, not only a resolution change
Design systems whose components are placed in slots of differing width (sidebar, main, card grid) and must adapt to the slot, not to the viewport
Progressive enhancement from a one-column phone layout upward, where no client-side JS is available on the smallest target
Migration off a separate mobile subdomain onto one URL set without losing the SEO equity or the mobile-specific content
avoid_when: The client is a known, fixed set of displays — kiosk, in-vehicle HMI, set-top box — where viewport negotiation adds cache variants for no variation
An internal tool with a single pinned browser and no mobile traffic; the negotiation machinery has no payoff
Pure API or data services with no presentation tier at all
Print-first or archival content where a fixed page geometry is the requirement
You cannot set `Vary` correctly at the caching layer — negotiation without correct cache keys is worse than no negotiation
component_types: Breakpoint ladder: the finite set of layout modes the design admits, chosen by viewport width or by container inline size
Media-query layer: viewport-condition CSS applied client-side with no second round trip and one cacheable document
Container-query context: a `container-type: inline-size` containment context plus `@container` rules, so a component adapts to its slot rather than to the window
Client-hint negotiator: the server's `Accept-CH` opt-in and the client's `Sec-CH-DPR`, `Sec-CH-Width`, `Sec-CH-Viewport-Width` request hints
Edge media transformer: a CDN or image service that derives resolution, format and crop variants on the fly from hints in the request
Adaptive origin / renderer: a server that renders a device-class-specific representation when the payload difference justifies leaving the document uncacheable
Representation cache: shared caches keyed on `Vary` over the negotiated hint headers, plus a URL scheme (file extension in the path) that the cache can key on
Capability-detection layer: feature probes and `@supports` used in preference to device identity when a decision is about capability rather than class
Design-system component set: the shared atoms/molecules/organisms that make one component library render correctly in every layout slot
technology_stack: HTTP Client Hints (Accept-CH, Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width)
imgix / Cloudinary / Cloudflare Images edge transformation
anti_patterns: Branching server behaviour on a parsed User-Agent string, which needs a device database maintained forever, misclassifies every new browser, and is trivially spoofable

Serving a separate m.example.com, which doubles every page, every front-end bug fix and every feature branch while the separate-sites guidance calls the approach conceptually simple but unmaintainable at any real feature-divergence point
Treating the User-Agent as an authorisation or security signal — it is client-supplied text and can be set to anything
Varying on a client hint without setting `Vary`, or with a `Vary` so wide that hit rate collapses; cache configuration is part of the pattern, not an afterthought
Using image URLs whose format is chosen by the query string rather than the path, which is the documented condition for a cache to bypass the response entirely
Shipping one large hero to every device because adaptation stopped at the layout layer and never reached the media layer
Writing media queries inside a reusable component, so the component's layout depends on the window instead of on the slot it was dropped into
Adapting layout with a JS resize listener that re-requests the document, when the same result is available in CSS with no network cost
Having three breakpoint systems — server branch, media query and container query — with no documented precedence between them
design_principles: Adaptation is a delivery-topology decision: choose where it happens (client, origin, edge) and pay the resulting cache and duplication cost knowingly
One URL space and one codebase beat N device-specific sites, because the maintenance cost of divergence is paid on every feature, not once
Cache key cardinality is a design output — every negotiated dimension multiplies it, so the `Vary` header is part of the architecture
Prefer capability detection and progressive enhancement to device identity, because UA strings lie and client hints are still incomplete
Components adapt to the container they occupy, not to the viewport, which is what makes one component set reusable across every layout
Serve the smallest correct representation; adaptation that stops at layout leaves the dominant cost (media bytes) untouched
best_practices: Send `Accept-CH` for the hints you actually consume and set `Vary` on exactly those hints, nothing more
Put the file extension in the image path rather than the query string so edge caches can key on the URL
Verify end-to-end that the negotiated response is a cache HIT under each hint value, not just that the right image came back
Design mobile-first with a single-column base layout and add breakpoints upward, so the smallest device is the baseline rather than a special case
Prefer container queries for anything inside a layout slot and reserve media queries for page-level chrome
Transform media at the edge from a single stored original instead of pre-generating and storing every variant
Test across breakpoints crossed with orientation and input modality, and include a no-JS path
Keep an explicit record of which dimensions are negotiated where, so a new device class is a configuration change rather than an archaeology exercise
references: W3C, Device Adaptation — Roadmap of Web Applications on Mobile, https://www.w3.org/Mobile/roadmap/adaptation.html

W3C, Responsive Design (Richard Davis / W3C talk, 2013) — server-side vs client-side adaptation, device description repositories, image pre-scaling, https://www.w3.org/2013/Talks/responsive-design.pdf

MDN Web Docs, Content negotiation — the standing drawbacks of server-driven negotiation (shared-cache efficiency, complexity, one header per dimension), https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Content_negotiation

MDN Web Docs, Browser detection using the user agent string (UA sniffing) — failure modes and the Client Hints alternative, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Browser_detection_using_the_user_agent
MDN Web Docs, @container — container queries and the containment context, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Containment/Container_queries
MDN Web Docs, Sec-CH-DPR header — Accept-CH opt-in, Content-DPR, Vary requirement, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Sec-CH-DPR
Cloudflare, Vary for images — file extension must be in the path or the cache bypasses the response, https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/advanced-configuration/vary-for-images
Cloudinary, Responsive images using client hints — CDN-level adaptation and returning `Vary: Sec-CH-DPR`, https://cloudinary.com/documentation/responsive_server_side_client_hints.md

imgix, Next-Generation Responsive Images with Client Hints — Accept-CH meta tag and hint-driven resizing, https://docs.imgix.com/en-US/getting-started/tutorials/responsive-design/next-generation-responsive-images-with-client-hints
Brad Frost, Atomic Design — the component hierarchy that makes one library reusable across layout slots, https://atomicdesign.bradfrost.com/chapter-2
